paragraphs: An agent learning in a changing environment needs to reuse past experience while adapting to new situations. These goals can conflict: a behavior that helped on one task may interfere with learning another, especially when the tasks demand contradictory actions. This paper addresses that interference alongside the broader problem of transferring useful knowledge across tasks.

The Bayesian Fast-Slow Framework maintains two policies with different sources of experience. The fast policy learns from recent data, giving it a route to respond to the current task. The slow policy learns through meta-reinforcement learning using data from previous tasks. A Bayesian estimation mechanism chooses between them, balancing exploration and exploitation as the agent learns.

The authors also add a dual-reset mechanism and data relabeling to the fast policy to accelerate convergence on new tasks. Their experiments report reduced interference and better performance than the evaluated baselines. The contribution is a framework that explicitly manages the tension between adapting locally and reusing accumulated experience, rather than treating all past learning as equally helpful.
neurips-2025-a-bayesian-fast-slow-framew.tldr: A Bayesian framework switches between policies trained on recent and historical experience to reduce interference as reinforcement-learning tasks change.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization involves an optimization problem whose solution depends on another optimization problem. In the setting studied here, the variables also lie on Riemannian manifolds, so their geometry matters when taking optimization steps. Existing approaches require advance information about derivatives and manifold curvature to choose step sizes, which can be difficult or computationally impractical to obtain.

The paper introduces Adaptive Riemannian Hypergradient Descent, or AdaRHD. Its central contribution is a fully adaptive step-size strategy that removes the need for those problem-specific parameters. This addresses a practical obstacle to applying existing methods: choosing how far to move without already knowing quantities that may be expensive to calculate.

The authors prove an iteration complexity of O(1/ε) for reaching an ε-stationary point, matching the stated bound for non-adaptive methods. This is a stationarity guarantee, not a claim of finding a global optimum. They also show that replacing exponential mappings with retraction mappings preserves the bound. Experiments report comparable performance to non-adaptive approaches with greater robustness, supporting the usefulness of adapting step sizes.
neurips-2025-an-adaptive-algorithm-for-b.tldr: AdaRHD adaptively chooses step sizes for Riemannian bilevel optimization while matching the iteration complexity of existing non-adaptive methods.

paragraphs: When a language model assigns a quality score, its final output may not capture all the useful information inside the network. This paper starts from preliminary evidence that middle-to-upper layers often contain representations that agree more closely with human judgments than the final layer does. It asks whether those internal signals can improve automated evaluation without fine-tuning the model.

LAGER is a post-processing framework for scoring individual responses. It combines score-token logits, the model's numerical signals for possible scores, across multiple layers. A softmax turns these signals into a distribution over scores, and LAGER computes the expected score. The backbone stays frozen, and the approach leaves the underlying inference process unchanged.

On Flask, HelpSteer, and BIGGen, the authors measure agreement with human scores using Spearman correlation and report improvements of up to 7.5% over the best baseline. Without reasoning steps, LAGER matches or exceeds the evaluated reasoning-based methods. Further experiments in data selection and emotional understanding support its generalization, suggesting that cross-layer information can improve how existing model judgments are read out.
neurips-2025-beyond-the-surface-enhancin.tldr: LAGER combines scoring signals from multiple internal LLM layers to improve agreement with human ratings without fine-tuning the backbone.

paragraphs: Binary integer programming expresses decisions using variables that can only be zero or one. Nonlinear relationships make these problems especially challenging. The paper identifies a scaling problem in approaches that use linear relaxations: representing nonlinear structure can cause exponential growth in auxiliary variables. BIPNN instead approaches the problem through an unsupervised hypergraph neural network.

The framework reformulates constrained, discrete problems, including those involving sine, logarithmic, and exponential terms, into unconstrained, differentiable polynomial losses. Its structural foundation is a one-to-one correspondence between polynomial binary objectives and hypergraphs. This correspondence provides a way to represent the optimization problem so that a hypergraph network can learn directly from its objective without labeled solutions.

A GPU-accelerated training pipeline combines gradient descent with continuous annealing to optimize large nonlinear terms in parallel and produce discrete, high-quality solutions. The authors report lower training costs and favorable results on synthetic and real-world datasets. The significance is the combination of problem reformulation, a matching network representation, and parallel optimization; the stated findings concern solution quality and efficiency rather than a universal guarantee of global optimality.
neurips-2025-bipnn-learning-to-solve-bin.tldr: BIPNN reformulates nonlinear binary optimization as differentiable polynomial losses and uses hypergraph networks to generate high-quality discrete solutions.

paragraphs: A recorded time series offers only a partial view of an underlying process that evolves continuously. Sensor constraints limit what is observed, while differences between domains become entangled with temporal patterns. This makes it difficult to learn representations that transfer across domains. EDEN addresses the problem by constructing multiple explicit views from the available data.

The framework expands the dataset across scales, feature subspaces, and time segments. Three coordinated modules use these views differently. Curriculum adaptation aligns domains progressively from coarse to fine scales. Quality-aware fusion assesses and combines temporal and frequency features from different subspaces. Temporal coherence learning encourages consistency across segments, bringing another source of structure into the representation.

Together, these views aim to approximate the hidden temporal patterns more accurately than a single sensor-limited view allows. The approach does not claim to directly observe the underlying continuous dynamics; it enriches the representations derived from discrete samples. Across six time-series benchmarks, the authors report consistent advantages and an average accuracy improvement of 4.8% over state-of-the-art methods in cross-domain settings.
neurips-2025-breakthrough-sensor-limited.tldr: EDEN combines multiple scales, feature subspaces, and temporal segments to improve time-series adaptation across domains.

paragraphs: A language model may stop stating a fact directly while retaining related information from which that fact can be inferred. This creates a problem for evaluating machine unlearning: testing isolated facts can make forgetting appear more complete than it is. The paper also emphasizes that knowledge in a model is not simply a deterministic present-or-absent property.

The authors introduce an evaluation framework that represents relevant factual contexts as knowledge graphs with confidence scores. The graph captures relationships among facts, while the scores represent confidence associated with that information. An inference-based protocol then uses LLM judges to reason over extracted subgraphs and assess whether the targeted knowledge has been successfully unlearned.

The judges use carefully designed prompts and are calibrated against human evaluations to support trustworthy, stable assessments. Experiments on a newly constructed benchmark indicate that this framework offers a more realistic and rigorous evaluation, and that current strategies tend to overestimate unlearning effectiveness. The contribution changes what counts as evidence of forgetting by examining correlated knowledge and inferential routes alongside explicit factual recall.
neurips-2025-do-llms-really-forget-evalu.tldr: A graph-based, confidence-aware evaluation finds that isolated-fact tests can overestimate how effectively LLMs forget knowledge.

paragraphs: Robotic manipulation often requires knowing how an object is making contact, not just recognizing its appearance or understanding an instruction. Vision-language-action models struggle when tasks demand precise force control, particularly under occlusion or dynamic uncertainty. ForceVLA addresses this by making external force sensing an explicit input to the action-generation system.

Its central component is a force-aware mixture-of-experts module called FVLMoE. During action decoding, the module combines pretrained visual-language representations with real-time six-axis force feedback. Context-dependent routing selects among experts associated with different modalities. This gives the action decoder a mechanism for adapting its use of sensory information to subtle changes in contact dynamics.

The paper also introduces ForceVLA-Data, which synchronizes vision, proprioception, and force-torque measurements across five contact-rich tasks. In the reported evaluation, ForceVLA improves average task success by 23.2% over strong π₀-based baselines and reaches up to 80% success on tasks such as plug insertion. These findings support incorporating force directly into multimodal action decoding for the evaluated manipulation settings.
neurips-2025-forcevla-enhancing-vla-mode.tldr: ForceVLA integrates real-time force feedback with vision and language through a mixture-of-experts module to improve contact-rich robotic manipulation.

paragraphs: Schrödinger bridges describe diffusion processes that move one probability distribution to another within a fixed time while minimizing a cost. Computing them often requires expensive training, even in small problems. This paper focuses on distributions represented as Gaussian mixtures and develops an analytic family of policies that can carry out the required distribution change.

The key simplification is to approximate the best policy within that family through a low-dimensional linear program, avoiding standard non-convex optimization. Its dimension scales linearly with the number of components in each mixture. The scope of the optimization matters: the paper approximates the optimum within its chosen feasible family, rather than claiming an unrestricted solution to every bridge problem.

The construction also extends to controllable linear time-varying systems and supports multi-marginal momentum bridges, which interpolate distributions subject to multiple marginals. Demonstrations include image translation in an autoencoder's latent space and learning cellular dynamics. These low-to-moderate-dimensional examples show the potential of combining an analytic policy representation with a compact optimization problem to reduce computational demands.
neurips-2025-go-with-the-flow-fast-diffu.tldr: An analytic policy family reduces diffusion between Gaussian mixtures to a small linear program that approximates the best policy within that family.

paragraphs: Large-scale 3D scene reconstruction with Gaussian splatting often divides a scene into separate pieces and optimizes them locally. That can lose information about the scene as a whole and introduce complicated choices about partitioning and tuning. MixGS takes a holistic approach, seeking to preserve global organization while still reconstructing fine details needed for rendering.

The framework combines camera pose information with Gaussian attributes in a view-aware representation. It then decodes that representation into detailed Gaussians. A mixing operation combines these decoded Gaussians with the original ones, allowing both forms to contribute to reconstruction. This is the mechanism the paper uses to jointly support global coherence and local fidelity.

Experiments on large scenes report state-of-the-art rendering quality, competitive speed, and substantially reduced computational requirements. The authors demonstrate training on a single GPU with 24 GB of video memory. The practical significance is that optimizing a scene holistically can be compatible with a constrained GPU memory budget, while delivering strong rendering results in the evaluated large-scale settings.
neurips-2025-holistic-large-scale-scene-.tldr: MixGS combines original and decoded Gaussians in a holistic scene representation, enabling high-quality large-scale reconstruction on a single 24 GB GPU.

paragraphs: Personalized practice requires both an estimate of what a student knows and exercises suited to that estimate. This paper joins those activities in a task called Knowledge-aware Exercise Generative Recommendation. The goal is to infer a student's evolving knowledge state from past exercise responses and generate customized new exercises, making practice both a diagnostic tool and a learning resource.

The proposed ExeGen framework coordinates four specialized agents responsible for supervision, knowledge-state perception, exercise generation, and quality refinement. They operate in an adaptive loop. For knowledge assessment, the system uses demonstration-based in-context learning to produce interpretable descriptions of student knowledge. A dual-matching strategy retrieves relevant demonstrations to support that reasoning.

For exercise creation, a group of quality-evaluation expert agents provides iterative adversarial feedback to refine generated material. This connects the assessment stage to a process for improving the resulting exercises. The authors develop an evaluation protocol and report favorable findings on real-world educational datasets and in a college deployment, supporting the effectiveness of this coordinated assessment-and-generation approach.
neurips-2025-knowledge-starts-with-pract.tldr: ExeGen coordinates LLM agents to infer student knowledge from exercise responses and iteratively generate and refine personalized practice.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents need to explore, but preset random exploration rules may respond poorly to the specifics of a task or the agent's changing learning status. The paper argues that simply reducing randomness over time provides limited flexibility. LLM-Explorer uses a language model to adapt the exploration process based on evidence from the agent's ongoing training.

The method samples the agent's learning trajectory and prompts an LLM to assess the current state of policy learning. The LLM then generates a probability distribution for future exploration. Periodically repeating this process produces a stochastic exploration strategy that changes with the task and learning progress, rather than following only a predetermined decay schedule.

LLM-Explorer is designed as a plug-in for algorithms including the DQN family, DDPG, TD3, and variants based on them. Experiments on Atari and MuJoCo report enhanced exploration and average performance improvements of up to 37.27%. These results support using LLM analysis to guide an existing reinforcement-learning algorithm's exploration, with the reported improvement remaining specific to the evaluated settings.
neurips-2025-llm-explorer-a-plug-in-rein.tldr: LLM-Explorer periodically uses an LLM to analyze learning trajectories and generate task-specific exploration distributions for reinforcement-learning agents.

paragraphs: Supervised transfer learning uses labeled data from a source distribution to help predictions on a target distribution. The source can be useful, but poorly matched source data can also hurt target performance. This paper studies how stochastic gradient descent can adaptively choose between source and target samples without knowing beforehand how helpful the source will be.

The proposed mixed-sample procedure changes its sampling behavior at individual optimization steps. Its theoretical foundation is an abstract sequence of constrained convex programs that preserves the desired statistical transfer guarantees. The authors establish that such a procedure is feasible for general prediction problems with convex losses, connecting efficient optimization to adaptation based on source quality.

For linear regression with squared loss, they provide a concrete instance that converges at a rate of 1/√T. The resulting solution's target statistical performance adapts to the initially unknown usefulness of the source data. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets support the theory. The contribution is an end-to-end account of how to optimize while gaining from informative source data and avoiding negative transfer from less informative data.
neurips-2025-mixed-sample-sgd-an-end-to-.tldr: Mixed-sample SGD adaptively draws source or target data while preserving transfer guarantees without prior knowledge of source quality.

paragraphs: A time series can be represented as numbers, images, or text, with each view exposing different patterns in the same signal. These representations also make pretrained large models available for forecasting. This paper examines a leading large-vision-model forecaster and identifies an inductive bias toward forecasting periods, then designs a framework intended to make productive use of that bias.

The framework, DMMV, organizes multiple views through decomposition. It combines trend-seasonal decomposition with an adaptive decomposition based on backcast residuals. These mechanisms separate aspects of the signal before integrating its representations for long-term forecasting. The key idea is to structure the multiple views around components of the time series, rather than relying on a single representation.

The authors compare DMMV with 14 state-of-the-art models across several datasets. It outperforms the evaluated single-view and existing multimodal baselines and achieves the best mean squared error on six of eight benchmark datasets. Those results support the usefulness of decomposition when adapting large vision models to forecasting, while showing that the best reported performance does not extend to every benchmark.
neurips-2025-multi-modal-view-enhanced-l.tldr: DMMV uses decomposition to combine multiple representations of time series, achieving the best forecasting MSE on six of eight benchmarks.

paragraphs: A scheduler may need to decide which jobs to run without knowing how long each will take. The objective here is to minimize the sum of job completion times. This paper adds a natural source of information to that setting: continuously updated progress bars that estimate the fraction of each job already completed.

The authors design algorithms for two ways of modeling that feedback. In the adversarial setting, progress information is treated through a worst-case perspective, and the algorithms receive competitive guarantees. These results also yield improved guarantees for learning-augmented scheduling based on job-size predictions. The paper additionally develops a general method for combining scheduling algorithms, contributing another tool for using predictive information.

A stochastic progress-bar model provides a more optimistic alternative to the worst-case setting. Within that model, the authors present an asymptotically optimal scheduling algorithm. The distinction between the two settings matters: the optimality claim belongs to the proposed stochastic model. Overall, the work formalizes how ongoing estimates of completion can improve scheduling even when processing times are initially unknown.
neurips-2025-non-clairvoyant-scheduling-.tldr: The paper develops scheduling algorithms with guarantees that use continuous progress estimates despite unknown job processing times.

paragraphs: A direct causal effect concerns how an exposure changes an outcome independently of pathways through a mediator. The weighted controlled direct effect averages over the mediator distribution, extending the standard controlled direct effect. This is useful when treatment effects differ across mediator levels and is relevant to fairness analysis, where separating direct and mediated influences can matter.

The paper first establishes necessary and sufficient conditions for uniquely identifying this weighted effect. It also clarifies when the weighted and standard controlled direct effects differ. Identification addresses whether the causal quantity can be uniquely determined; the next question is how precisely it can be estimated once that is possible.

To address precision, the authors derive the efficient influence function and study regular, asymptotically linear estimators. They characterize the covariate adjustment set that minimizes asymptotic variance within this setting. Interactions between mediators and confounders create requirements distinct from those for estimating average treatment effects. The contribution therefore connects identification with principled adjustment choices for efficient direct-effect estimation in fairness and mediation analysis.
neurips-2025-optimal-adjustment-sets-for.tldr: The paper establishes identifiability conditions and variance-minimizing covariate adjustment sets for estimating weighted controlled direct effects.

paragraphs: A deployed classifier can encounter inputs unlike those represented in its training distribution. Detecting such inputs can support abstention instead of an unreliable decision. This paper develops an out-of-distribution score based on angles, motivated by the observation that distance-focused methods may overlook or inadequately use the structure of familiar, in-distribution data.

The score measures angles involving feature representations and decision boundaries, using the mean of in-distribution features as the viewpoint. This makes the comparison relative to the geometry of familiar data. The authors show that these angles provide a useful signal for separating in-distribution and out-of-distribution examples, offering a different use of learned feature geometry.

Across nine ImageNet-pretrained models, the method achieves the lowest false-positive rate on five, the best average rate overall, and a top-three ranking on every evaluated model. Results with ResNet SCL and CLIP also highlight benefits from contrastive representations. Finally, the score's scale invariance enables an ensemble formed by simply summing scores, providing a straightforward way to combine detection signals.
neurips-2025-out-of-distribution-detecti.tldr: An angle-based score anchored at the mean of familiar features improves out-of-distribution detection across evaluated ImageNet models.

paragraphs: Real-world super-resolution aims to improve images captured outside controlled settings, including phone photographs. Large generative models can produce strong results, but their computation and latency complicate edge deployment. PocketSR is a single-step model designed to retain generative image-enhancement capabilities while substantially reducing the computational burden and preserving fidelity.

The authors replace the expensive Stable Diffusion variational autoencoder with LiteED, an encoding-and-decoding component that uses 97.5% fewer parameters while preserving high-quality transformations. They also introduce online annealing pruning for the U-Net. This progressively transfers generative priors from heavy modules to lighter ones, with a multi-layer feature-distillation loss helping retain prior knowledge during pruning.

The resulting model has 146 million parameters and is reported to process a 4K image in 0.8 seconds. Its evaluated performance is comparable to state-of-the-art single-step and even multi-step super-resolution models. The contribution combines a smaller image representation component with gradual pruning and knowledge transfer, showing how several coordinated efficiency changes can preserve strong enhancement quality in the reported evaluation.
neurips-2025-pocketsr-the-super-resoluti.tldr: PocketSR combines efficient encoding, gradual pruning, and feature distillation to deliver single-step image super-resolution with substantially reduced computation.

paragraphs: Predicting whether two proteins interact does not by itself establish that a model can reconstruct a biologically useful interaction network. PRING addresses that evaluation gap by moving from isolated pairs to graph-level assessment. Its dataset spans multiple species and contains 21,484 proteins and 186,818 interactions, with strategies designed to address redundancy and data leakage.

The benchmark offers two complementary evaluation perspectives. Topology-oriented tasks examine network construction within and across species. Function-oriented tasks assess protein complexes and pathways, Gene Ontology modules, and essential proteins. Together, these tasks test both the organization of predicted connections and their relevance to biological functions, connecting interaction prediction to the uses researchers want from a network.

The authors evaluate four categories of approaches: sequence similarity, naive sequence models, protein language models, and structure-based methods. Their experiments reveal potential limitations in recovering both structural and functional network properties. PRING therefore provides evidence of a gap between promising pairwise prediction and support for real biological applications, while supplying a benchmark for measuring progress on that broader goal.
neurips-2025-pring-rethinking-protein-pr.tldr: PRING evaluates whether protein-interaction predictors reconstruct biologically meaningful networks, revealing gaps beyond isolated pairwise prediction.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning with risk-averse objectives based on total reward over an undiscounted, infinite horizon. The focus is on the entropic risk measure and entropic value-at-risk. Existing model-based algorithms can handle small problems, but they require complete access to transition probabilities, making that information requirement a central obstacle.

The authors propose a Q-learning algorithm for computing an optimal stationary policy for these objectives. Two properties of the entropic risk measure support the construction and its optimality: dynamic consistency and elicitability. These properties are central to making the proposed learning approach work for the stated risk-sensitive total-reward setting.

The paper supplies strong convergence and performance guarantees, together with numerical experiments in tabular domains. Those experiments show quick and reliable convergence to the optimal risk-averse value function. The contribution is both algorithmic and theoretical: it provides a Q-learning route for objectives previously addressed by algorithms needing full transition probabilities, while its reported numerical evidence concerns tabular problems.
neurips-2025-risk-averse-total-reward-re.tldr: A Q-learning algorithm learns optimal stationary policies for risk-averse, undiscounted total-reward objectives with convergence and performance guarantees.

paragraphs: Training robotic hands is difficult because collecting demonstrations is demanding and controlling many joints creates a large search space. Reinforcement learning can generate experience in simulation, but often depends on carefully crafted rewards or reference motions. This paper asks whether coarse guidance from a vision-language model can supply enough structure for reinforcement learning to refine the details.

Given a task description and a visual scene, an off-the-shelf vision-language model identifies relevant keypoints, such as handles or buttons. It then generates three-dimensional trajectories for both the hand and the object. These trajectories serve as scaffolds. A low-level residual reinforcement-learning policy is trained in simulation to track them with high fidelity.

The division of work is central: the vision-language model supplies spatial and semantic guidance, while reinforcement learning refines the motion. Across simulated tasks involving articulated objects and semantic understanding, the authors report robust learned manipulation policies. They also demonstrate transfer to real robotic hands without human demonstrations or handcrafted rewards, supporting the usefulness of coarse generated trajectories as training guidance.
neurips-2025-scaffolding-dexterous-manip.tldr: A vision-language model generates coarse hand and object trajectories that guide reinforcement learning for dexterous manipulation and demonstrated real-world transfer.

paragraphs: Generating the weights of a neural network becomes difficult as the target network grows. Recurrent Diffusion for Large-Scale Parameter Generation, or RPG, tackles this scaling problem by generating network parameters at sizes reaching hundreds of millions on a single GPU. The framework organizes weight generation into smaller pieces while learning relationships among them.

RPG partitions a network's parameters into non-overlapping tokens, each representing a distinct portion of the model. A recurrent mechanism learns how these tokens relate and produces prototypes. Those prototypes condition a diffusion process that synthesizes the parameters. This organization allows the framework to model dependencies across parameter groups without treating the entire parameter collection as an undivided object.

Across the tested architectures and tasks, including ResNets, ConvNeXts, ViTs, and LoRA-based language models, the generated parameters deliver performance comparable to fully trained networks without excessive memory overhead. The authors also report valid parameter generation for previously unseen tasks. These findings support the possibility of scalable weight generation, with demonstrated generalization beyond the generator's training tasks.
neurips-2025-scaling-up-parameter-genera.tldr: RPG combines recurrent modeling of parameter groups with conditioned diffusion to generate large neural-network weights on a single GPU.

paragraphs: Physics questions can require a model to extract information from a diagram and connect it to physical reasoning. SeePhys is a benchmark designed to test that combination. Its questions range from middle-school material to PhD qualifying exams, cover seven fundamental physics domains, and include 21 categories of diagrams with varied visual forms.

A defining feature is that 75% of the problems require visual information for a correct solution. This makes the images essential parts of the reasoning task rather than mainly supporting illustrations. The benchmark therefore tests whether a model can use what a diagram communicates when the text alone is insufficient.

In the authors' evaluation, even advanced visual reasoning models, including Gemini-2.5-pro and o4-mini, score below 60% accuracy. Their analysis identifies difficulties in tightly connecting diagram interpretation with physics reasoning and a persistent tendency to rely on textual cues as shortcuts. These findings show that the evaluated models still face substantial challenges on physics problems where successful reasoning depends on correctly understanding the visual evidence.
neurips-2025-seephys-does-seeing-help-th.tldr: SeePhys tests physics reasoning that depends on diagrams, with evaluated advanced visual reasoning models achieving less than 60% accuracy.

paragraphs: Neural speech decoding aims to translate brain activity into communication for people with severe paralysis. This paper works with a benchmark containing intracranial recordings from a paralyzed participant attempting speech. It targets a practical challenge: improving decoding accuracy while keeping computation low enough for real-time use and maintaining performance across different recording days.

The approach combines three changes. Training uses extensive time masking, hiding more than half of each trial on average. A compact Transformer replaces the baseline gated recurrent unit network. Finally, a lightweight test-time adaptation method updates the decoder using several time-masked versions of a single trial, requiring only one gradient step per trial.

Compared with the baseline GRU, the Transformer uses 83% fewer parameters, reduces peak GPU memory by 52%, and calibrates significantly faster. Together, the changes reduce word error rate by 20% and mitigate degradation on held-out days in a real-time decoding setting. The results connect accuracy improvements with lower computational costs on this participant-based benchmark, rather than assessing accuracy independently of deployment demands.
neurips-2025-time-masked-transformers-wi.tldr: Extensive time masking, a compact Transformer, and one-step test-time adaptation improve real-time neural speech decoding while reducing computation.

paragraphs: Video face swapping must preserve identity and appearance consistently across frames, including when faces turn or become partly hidden. Methods trained primarily on still images struggle with those temporal demands. VividFace combines static image data with video sequences in a hybrid training strategy, using a diffusion model and a specialized variational autoencoder to process both kinds of input efficiently.

The paper also introduces the Attribute-Identity Disentanglement Triplet dataset. Each triplet contains three face images arranged so that two share a pose and two share an identity. This structure supports separating identity from pose. Occlusion augmentation helps improve robustness to hidden facial regions, while three-dimensional reconstruction provides conditioning information for handling large pose changes.

Experiments report state-of-the-art identity preservation, temporal consistency, and visual realism, alongside fewer inference steps than existing methods. The framework reduces flickering, identity loss, and sensitivity to occlusions and pose variation in the evaluated settings. Its contribution brings together temporal training, structured identity-pose data, and geometric conditioning to address several linked sources of video inconsistency.
neurips-2025-vividface-a-robost-and-high.tldr: VividFace combines image-video training, identity-pose triplets, and 3D conditioning to improve the realism and temporal consistency of video face swaps.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks often spend substantial training time repeatedly passing messages across all nodes. YOSO exploits the observation that features and embeddings on many real-world graphs have sparse representations in the graph Fourier domain. If much of the relevant signal can be represented compactly there, computation can move into a smaller spectral space.

The method applies one graph Fourier transformation, projecting features onto a learnable orthonormal basis and retaining M coefficients for a graph with N nodes, where M is much smaller than N. Network computation then takes place in that reduced domain. Full-graph embeddings are reconstructed only at the output through a bounded optimization problem with ℓ₂,₁ regularization.

The recovery argument draws on compressed sensing. For k-row-sparse spectra, the authors show that the learned-basis projection can satisfy the restricted isometry property with M = O(k log N), supporting stable recovery during training. This is a sparsity-dependent theoretical result. Empirically, YOSO reduces training time by 74% on average across five benchmarks relative to state-of-the-art methods while maintaining competitive accuracy.
neurips-2025-you-only-spectralize-once-t.tldr: YOSO trains graph neural networks in a compressed spectral space, reducing average training time by 74% across five benchmarks while retaining competitive accuracy.
